data.title: 'Treasonous scum': Trump attacks media over Iran war coverage
data.description:
President Trump is attacking news organizations reporting on the strain the Iran war has placed on America’s weapons stockpiles, calling those outlets “treasonous” and accusing them of wanting the U.S. to lose because they specifically don’t want to see him win.  

He took to Truth Social to vent, writing: “The people and Media Outlets that keep harping on the fact that we have no ammunition (And they are 100% wrong!), are actually treasonous. They do it because they would rather see the United States LOSE a War that we’re easily WINNING, than see me WIN!”  

He went on, saying: “For the treasonous SCUM that refuses to accurately report on our Military Operation in Iran, we have virtually unlimited amounts of Mid to High Grade Ammunition, far more than we could ever use for this, or for any other War”  

But reporting from multiple outlets paints a very different picture.  

The Hill points to an estimate from analysts at the Center for Strategic and International Studies that shows by late July, the U.S. had an estimated 759 to 827 Patriot interceptors remaining — down from roughly 2,330 before the war.   

The Washington Post this week reported that senior military officials warned Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that continuing the current pace of operations could become unsustainable and limit America’s ability to respond to threats elsewhere, even here in America.  

And reportedly, some military leaders issued what are known as “non-concurs,” essentially putting their disagreement on the record while still following orders. According to the report, the Navy, in particular, is facing significant strain, with its top admiral reportedly warning that the service cannot sustain the current level of support without an anticipated end date.  

The Army’s top civilian leader, Secretary Daniel P. Driscoll, quit this week, handing in his resignation after repeatedly clashing with Hegseth due to his firing or forcing out more than a dozen senior military officers and generals during his tenure.  

Many Americans disagreed with the decision to go to war. We were also told this war was not supposed to be open-ended. The administration initially talked about a roughly six-week timeline. We are now in the seventh month.  

Nobody wants to see the United States fail. Nobody wants American service members put in greater danger. Nobody wants our military unprepared to respond to another threat. But that does not mean Americans have to pretend this war is going according to plan. 

This was a war of choice. The administration bypassed Congress to enter it, and now Americans are being asked to trust the administration’s assessment of progress while questions about weapons, readiness, military deployments and an endgame continue to mount. You can support the troops and still question the mission. If the goal still is actually to bring this conflict to an end, the administration owes the American people more than all caps messages on Truth Social. Provide us with an objective and an exit strategy. 

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

data.title: WNBA commissioner stepping down after this season
data.description:
(NewsNation) — WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert is retiring at the end of the year, following seven years in the role.

NBA Commissioner Adam Silver announced the news Friday.

“Cathy has presided over the WNBA through the most significant period of growth in the league’s 30-year history,” Silver wrote in a statement. “We are grateful for Cathy’s leadership and unwavering commitment to the advancement of women’s basketball.”

With Engelbert at the helm, the WNBA expanded from 12 teams to 18 by the end of 2030. Transformative media rights and collective bargaining agreements also led to increases in salaries and benefits for athletes.

“In 2019, I had the privilege of being appointed the league’s first commissioner and to lead a league with enormous potential yet untapped awareness and significant undervaluation,” Englebert said. “Over the years, it has been amazing to watch WNBA players thrive and lead the massive cultural surge around women’s sports.”

However, the commissioner was also criticized by players for her lack of connection to the league and her leadership style.

Recently, she said the league would continue to have discussions regarding transgender athletes, an issue which has become a major one for Republican lawmakers. She called it a complex and nuanced issue, saying in a memo that the league would continue discussions on the topic.

That memo came after two former NBA players, Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White, declared themselves to be eligible for the WNBA draft because they identified as women.

Engelbert also took criticism for the number of hard fouls Caitlyn Clark, a prodigious player and among the most popular female athletes on the planet, has taken in her first three seasons in the league.

The outgoing commissioner is expected to lead a succession plan and has submitted a list of candidates to take over the role for consideration.

Bobby Oler contributed to this report.

data.title: NC elections officials alter mail ballot rules just before they're mailed out
data.description:
The North Carolina State Board of Elections approved new guidelines Friday regarding mail-in ballots, hours before those same ballots were sent to voters.

The new guideline pertains to the standards the board will be using to decide whether to count a mail-in ballot — including requiring officials to disqualify a ballot if the ballot’s signature does not match the name assigned to the application on the return envelope.

Other changes specify that only a voter’s near relative or legal guardian can deliver their mail-in ballot in-person on their behalf and require officials to disqualify ballots if more than one is included in one return envelope.

The new guidelines were debated between board officials with the two lone Democrats dissenting on the decision. 

“To my mind, we’re doing an end run around the process that we said we wanted to do,” Democratic member Siobhan Millen said at the board’s meeting. “It may not affect you as you’re filling it out, but it affects whether your ballot counts — that’s huge. So, an effort to say this is just a process thing, I think is incorrect.”

Stacy Eggers, a Republican member of the board, defended the new standards, saying, “This is simply guidance, updated guidance, I might add, as to what the board and staff at the county level will do and how they will process things.”

The guidelines were approved as numbered memos after similar rulings from the board couldn’t go into effect despite the state’s Rules Review Commission unanimously approving it due to a provision in state law that delays such rules if 10 or more formal objections are received.

The previous rulings must be decided by the North Carolina legislature in its next session.

The first batch of ballots were initially promised to be sent out to more than 46,000 voters even as the ballot’s validity is still being decided at the federal level.

The Justice Department asked the Supreme Court on Thursday to clear the way for the U.S. Postal Service (USPS) to implement President Trump’s executive order targeting mail voting in time for the midterms. 

USPS’s plan would mandate that states’ mail-in ballots meet design requirements — such as unique barcodes and an official logo — and require election officials to upload lists of voters who are eligible to vote by mail otherwise USPS will refuse to deliver ballots. 

In a filing last week, North Carolina Assistant Deputy Attorney General Marc Brunton argued against the USPS rules due to “the very short time available and the untested technology that the Rule relies on.”

He argued that the mail-in ballot system was “particularly important” for parts of Western North Carolina in the wake of Hurricane Helene which severely hurt the region in 2024 – with damages across the state reportedly totaling to $60 billion.

data.title: The veteran community cannot wait: Pass the take care of America's Veterans Act now
data.description:
For more than three decades in the Air Force, my mission was taking care of our people. As the service’s senior officer for manpower and personnel, I answered for the well-being of airmen and their families. Shortly after retiring in 2022, I began my next mission: Leading the Military Officers Association of America. More than 350,000 members strong, MOAA works to protect the earned benefits of all who serve and have served, along with their families and their survivors, across all ranks and uniformed services.

As part of this work, I am urging Congress to pass the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act to keep this nation’s promises to our veterans, to the caregivers who sustain them, and to the survivors who carry their legacy.

The bill includes one of MOAA’s top priorities: The Major Richard Star Act, which would end an unjust offset forcing more than 59,000 combat-injured veterans to forfeit earned retirement pay. Many of our members, and those they led, have waited years for this fix.

But there is much more to the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act. The bill gathers more than 60 pieces of legislation — almost all bipartisan, and many have been stalled in Congress for years. Together, they would help family caregivers rebuild their financial and professional futures after years of sacrifice in support of veterans. They would allow surviving spouses to retain critical benefits by removing arcane remarriage penalties, and increase Dependency and Indemnity Compensation for all survivors, with special attention to ensuring surviving spouses of veterans with ALS receive the benefits they deserve. And they would fund community programs working to prevent veteran suicide.

MOAA is one of more than 20 stakeholder organizations that support this legislation. A recent survey by Mission Roll Call found 71 percent of veterans feel the same.

The bill is not without its flaws, and the misconceptions surrounding it deserve a direct answer. The mechanism used to pay for these worthy, long-overdue programs is far from perfect. But the bill ensures projected savings created by changes to the VA disability system regarding sleep apnea and tinnitus — changes already in motion at the VA — will remain within the veteran community. Failing to take advantage of this unique but fleeting legislative opportunity not only costs us the chance to enact dozens of meaningful changes, but it also means any savings from these imminent rule changes will be returned to the Treasury.

No veteran will see existing benefits reduced if this bill passes. No disability ratings will drop, and no treatment plans will be altered or interrupted. Future veterans will retain access to VA care for service-connected injuries like tinnitus and sleep apnea — the rating process will change, but they will not be marginalized or abandoned.

The only true threat to earned benefits is continued inaction, where combat-injured retirees keep losing pay they have earned, caregivers cannot return to the workforce, and survivors struggle to rebuild their lives without full and fair compensation for their service member’s sacrifice. These are not hypotheticals — they are realities facing service members, families, and survivors of those serving right now in the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. I worry far more about inaction costing them the support they need and earned than I do about them seeing adjusted disability ratings down the road.

Nearly all the bill’s measures have been introduced in both chambers, under Republican and Democratic majorities alike, only to stall again and again across congresses and administrations. Keeping promises to those who served is not partisan. Backing this bill, imperfections and all, is not a political act; it is a pragmatic one. It honors the current service members and veterans who gave so much, the caregivers and families who carry the weight beside them, and the survivors who keep their memory alive.

Failure to take advantage of this unique opportunity sends them back to square one with nothing to show but another year of frustration and no clear path to passing and funding these key pieces of legislation. If you set politics, emotion, and organizational interests aside and truly take a veteran-centric approach, the answer becomes clearer, and things get better for tens of millions of veterans, caregivers and survivors.

I urge Congress to pass the Take Care of America’s Veterans Act now. Those who wear and those who wore the uniform kept every promise they made to this country. The most patriotic thing we can do is keep ours.

Lt. Gen. Brian T. Kelly, USAF (Ret), is president and CEO of the Military Officers Association of America (MOAA), the nation’s largest association of military officers, and served 33 years in the Air Force, including as deputy chief of staff for manpower, personnel, and services.

data.title: Nearly a third of AI chatbot replies to voting questions inaccurate, outdated: Study
data.description:
Artificial intelligence chatbots are becoming a new source for voters to ask questions about upcoming elections, but a new study determined nearly a third of AI-generated replies could be inaccurate or outdated. 

In a report released Thursday, researchers with the Institute for Strategic Dialogue (ISD) tested 15 different generic prompts across six AI chatbots, and found 29 percent of responses were incomplete, inaccurate or outdated. Generic questions included topics like mail-in voting, voter registration and important dates. 

Errors included misidentifying Election Day dates, showing outdated requirements and deadlines, according to the report.

In 16 percent of the replies, the chatbot answered correctly but did not include important information that could be useful to a voter, such as key deadlines or ways to prove identity. 

The models tested included Meta’s Muse Spark, xAI’s Grok 4.3, DeepSeek’s V4 Pro, OpenAI’s GPT-5.5, Anthropic’s Sonnect 4.6 and Google’s Gemini 3.5 Flash.

The ISD, which focuses on extremism, disinformation and online threats, tailored the prompts to ten states with a history of electoral process changes, related legislation or election administration controversy. 

“As LLMs play a larger role in shaping the information environment, the reliability and behavior of these systems will increasingly affect voter access and trust,” ISD researchers wrote. “This analysis finds that models’ overall accuracy on election process is mixed, and concerns remain over a reliance on outdated sources, overconfidence in relaying nuanced and conditional information, and performance divergences between languages.”

OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 was deemed the most accurate model, answering 89 percent of the responses with specific, complete and correct information. Gemini 3.5 Flash came in second, answering 84 percent of questions accurately, while Grok 4.3 fell behind at 66 percent, Sonnet 4.6 at 64 percent, DeepSeek at 63 percent and Musk Spark at 61 percent. 

Researchers said all of the models also returned some outdated information, though DeepSeek — made by a Chinese AI startup — showed the most outdated information, such as referencing 2024 election dates. 

The accuracy drastically plummeted 16 percent when prompted in Spanish, researchers noted.  Answers in Spanish were also 6 percent more likely to be outdated or inaccurate, with every model’s performance dropping for the language. 

When researchers tested for “adversarial claims,” all six models refuted false or misleading claims at high rates when asked in English, though the rates were mostly similar in Spanish as well. Muse Spark and Gemini had the most ambiguous or hedging responses, at 22 and 18 percent, respectively. 

Despite concerns over accuracy, researchers said many of their findings are “encouraging,” as the large language models largely cited authoritative sources for answers and “effectively confront[ed]” false claims at high rates. 

Except for Meta, researchers tested the models through their application programming interfaces (APIs), which are made for developers and can differ from the consumer-facing software most of the public uses. 

A spokesperson for Google’s Gemini pointed to this when reached for comment, stating the consumer version of the model “has different protections and is how most people use our AI.” They also pointed to the disclaimer shown on the Gemini app, which states, “Election info changes quickly. Verify responses with official sources.” 

“Gemini is designed to respond with accurate and timely information and performed well in this analysis,” the spokesperson added. 

For Meta, analysts used “clean research accounts without links to existing Meta accounts,” according to the report. 

When asked about the report, OpenAI maintained its focus on securing AI systems ahead of elections. 

“As elections take place around the world, we are committed to continuing to elevate accurate voting information, combat misuse by bad actors, and increase transparency,” the spokesperson said. 

xAI, DeepSeek, Meta and Anthropic did not respond to a request for comment. 

Researchers laid out a series of recommendations to counter concerns with AI models. They urged election officials and civil society organizations to treat official websites as a direct input into these models and update them frequently.

They also asked model developers to reduce a models’ overconfidence when responding to conditional or ongoing election questions, and “close the language gap.”

data.title: Live updates: Judge ready to declare mistrial in Clancy trial; August posts strong jobs numbers
data.description:
The judge in the Lindsay Clancy murder case announced Friday that he was declaring a mistrial after jurors were unable to reach a unanimous verdict. However, when defense attorney Kevin Reddington requested an immediate stay of the declaration, the judge gave the defense one hour to appeal.

North Carolina is set to begin mailing general election absentee ballots on Friday, even as the Trump administration has moved to restrict voting by mail.

The administration is appealing a federal judge’s ruling that stops it from moving forward with voting restrictions established by executive order for at least for one more week. The Justice Department asked the Supreme Court on Thursday to lift the block.

And North Carolina’s State Board of Elections will meet at 9 a.m. EDT to offer guidance on mailing ballots.

The U.S. economy added 162,000 jobs last month, a stronger-than-expected showing.

Stars and Stripes staffers whom the Pentagon wants to fire will be in a Washington court on Friday morning to fight the termination notices.

President Trump has a policy meeting and will sign an executive order on Friday before heading to New Jersey for the holiday weekend.

Follow along live below.

data.title: Venezuela is the blueprint for what Washington will demand from Iran
data.description:
Washington’s announcement last week — claiming 55 percent control of a new venture holding more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan crude, under field concessions U.S. officials say could last a century, part of a wider energy accord — looked, at first glance, like a regional story. A post-Maduro resource deal in America’s backyard.

But Venezuela isn’t the headline. It is the template. And it quietly answers a question that has hung over Iran policy for months: What does this administration actually consider a win?

The answer starts with a simple observation: Washington is running two campaigns against oil-producing adversaries, and they increasingly resemble two versions of the same strategy. In Venezuela, the U.S. used force — a military operation, a captured president, and an interim government willing to sign away a century of oil-field access within seven months. In Iran, that kind of decapitation was never plausible. Six months into open conflict, Tehran has absorbed the pressure and has not cracked.

So Washington shifted to the tool it has left: economic strangulation. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s Operation Economic Outcast mirrors the Venezuela playbook in tone and ambition, promising to sever “every economic lifeline” sustaining Tehran — with China, Iran’s largest oil buyer, placed squarely in the crosshairs.

That detail is the real connective tissue. Both operations share a secondary objective that has nothing to do with ideology and everything to do with market power: cutting China off from discounted, sanctions-adjacent crude. Venezuela’s joint venture displaces China as the biggest customer of its state oil company. The Iran sanctions campaign targets Beijing’s position as Tehran’s largest trading partner.

This, more than any sweeping theory of a “Trump doctrine,” explains his current actions. And this thesis can be tested: watch whether secondary-sanctions deadlines for Chinese buyers and shippers are actually enforced, or quietly softened once Beijing signals real retaliation.

The more revealing question is what Venezuela tells us about the terms Washington will seek if Iran is eventually brought back to the table. Sanctions are usually sold as leverage toward narrow outcomes: ending the war, rolling back the nuclear program. But Venezuela shows that when this administration holds real leverage over an oil-producing state, it doesn’t stop at policy concessions. It converts leverage into ownership.

If Iran returns to negotiations under economic exhaustion, the model on Washington’s desk won’t be the 2015 nuclear-deal framework of sanctions relief for inspections. It will look more like Caracas: American capital and off-take rights embedded directly in Iranian energy infrastructure, framed as reconstruction investment rather than war spoils — and sold domestically as costing U.S. taxpayers nothing.

That vision deserves skepticism. Iran is not Venezuela. There is no captured leader, no Delcy Rodríguez-style interim government willing to sign a century-long concession. Any equity transfer would require either a sweeping settlement far beyond anything currently on the table or an outright regime collapse, neither close to a base case today.

History cuts against the idea too. Sanctioned states under real strain — Iran under the 2015 deal, Iraq in the 1990s, Russia since 2022 — have endured contraction, inflation, and discounted exports before surrendering core state assets. Equity-for-relief has no real precedent absent a compliant client government, which Washington has in Caracas but not in Tehran.

Iran’s oil sector is also far less degraded than Venezuela’s, and Tehran has spent two decades building alternatives to reduce its dependence on Washington’s goodwill. Any deal resembling Venezuela’s would collide with a deeper obstacle still: the legacy of the 1951 nationalization under Mohammad Mossadegh, which made resource sovereignty politically sacred across Iran’s factions, a barrier Venezuela’s constitutional language doesn’t approach.

Even Venezuela’s own precedent may not survive. Its constitution assigns the state primary ownership of hydrocarbons, and a century-long concession signed by an unelected government is exactly the kind of claim a future elected one could void. A model that may not endure in Caracas is a shaky template to export to Tehran.

These differences matter, and they’re why nothing resembling the Venezuela deal is likely in Iran anytime soon. But they don’t invalidate the comparison, they define it. The honest version of this argument isn’t that Washington will replicate Caracas in Tehran. It’s that the Venezuela deal has given this administration a working precedent for converting leverage into resource control when political conditions allow it — tested once, sold successfully at home — and that precedent will shape how negotiators define a favorable outcome the next time Washington holds real cards against an oil state, Iran included.

The question worth watching isn’t whether Tehran signs a century-long concession next month. It’s whether the language of “reconstruction investment” and “sanctions-relief partnership” begins showing up in any future Iran negotiating track. If it does, Venezuela will be the reason we already know what it means.

Charbel A. Antoun is a Washington-based journalist and writer specializing in U.S. foreign policy, with a focus on the Middle East and North Africa.

data.title: Trump threatens trade war if rates aren't cut after strong jobs report
data.description:
President Trump called on the Federal Reserve to lower interest rates Friday after the August jobs report came in stronger than expected, threatening to cut off trade with several countries if the central bank doesn’t budge.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday that U.S. employers added 162,000 jobs last month, well above the 53,000 that economists were anticipating.

Trump touted the “great” jobs numbers Friday before quickly turning his attention to the Fed, which he has long pushed to slash rates.

“Lower the interest rates because the U.S.A. is a much stronger credit than it was just a short time ago!” he wrote in a post on Truth Social. “A STRONG COUNTRY MEANS A LOWER INTEREST RATE – IT’S A BETTER CREDIT.”

“Without the United States agreeing to allow them their big surpluses, and we could stop that immediately, they would no longer be considered financially ELITE!” he added. “LOWER THE RATE OR I’LL STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT.”

The Fed has held rates steady at a range of 3.5 to 3.75 percent at its last five meetings, as inflation has remained persistently above the central bank’s target rate of 2 percent.

Annual inflation sat at 3.7 percent year-over-year in July, according to the personal consumer expenditures (PCE) price index, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation.

However, Friday’s job numbers appear to increase the chances that the central bank raises rather than lowers rates. The latest data alleviates concerns that higher rates are weakening the labor market and allows the Fed to turn its attention to curtailing inflation.

Traders are now pricing in a 60 percent chance that the Fed hikes rates by a quarter point at its next meeting this month, according to CME FedWatch, which tracks bets placed on future central bank decisions.

Trump touted Fed Chair Kevin Warsh as a “great new leader” Friday even as he ramped up pressure on his pick to run the central bank. The president frequently feuded with Warsh’s predecessor, Jerome Powell, over rate cuts, threatening to fire him on several occasions.

“The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart – BE PATRIOTS for a change,” Trump said. “High interest rates put the U.S.A. at a very unfair disadvantage, and I won’t allow that to happen!”

data.title: Fetterman stood up disabled veterans; scoffed at children's hospital's concerns: Report
data.description:
Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) reportedly cancelled a meeting with three disabled veterans almost a year after he dismissed concerns about funding concerns for a children’s hospital.

The Wall Street Journal published a report Wednesday that alleged the first-term Senator faked an illness to avoid meeting with the veterans, later opting to do an interview with Fox News on Israel and the war in Iran in seemingly good health.

Fetterman – who reportedly went for almost a year without participating in a public event in Pennsylvania – tried to also dodge a meeting with the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP).

In 2025 messages with an aide, Fetterman questioned continual meetings with CHOP, writing, “Why do I have to keep having to meet with CHOP?”

“Because they are worried about vaccines and Medicaid cuts,” the aide answered.

“Well I’m not,” Fetterman wrote. “I’m convinced they just want free trips to DC.”

A report from Public Citizen in March found that the One Big, Beautiful Bill Act package last year that cut Medicaid funding put more than 400 hospitals across the country in danger of closing or reducing services.

Fetterman at the time voted against the package which included Medicaid funding cuts, saying, “I’ll keep fighting to protect health care.”

Other alleged messages from 2025, appeared to show Fetterman backing out of a funeral for police officers who were killed in the Keystone State – citing the event’s length. 

“3 hours??” Fetterman texted. 

“Yes it’s a very formal ceremony and the equivalent of 3 separate funerals,” an aide wrote back.

“This may be a nonstarter,” Fetterman responded.

The three officers were killed in the line of duty while attempting to serve a warrant in North Codorus Township at the time – miles away from Fetterman’s hometown. 

The WSJ report noted that for the past year, Fetterman attended 26 of the 31 full hearings for his assigned committees but did not speak in 20 of them. 

Fetterman’s office did not respond to The Hill’s request for immediate comment on the report.

Pennsylvania Democrats have voiced outrage about the report, with Rep. Brendan Boyle (D-Pa.) calling Fetterman “a disgrace.”

“Our state deserves better than a lazy trust fund baby who is too lazy to do the job,” Boyle said on social platform X.

While the senator is not up for re-election in this midterm cycle, Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.) said on Thursday, “Pennsylvania will do something about it in 2028.”

data.title: Republicans face a dilemma over Trump's role in the midterms
data.description:
All 435 House seats, along with 35 seats in the Senate (including special elections in Florida and Ohio), will be up for grabs in the midterm elections. President Trump’s name will not be on any of those ballots. Not a single one.

And yet just about every Democrat will be running against him.

Midterm elections are a report card on how the president is doing — and voters almost always decide the president, any president, isn’t doing a good enough job. That is why the president’s party almost always loses seats in Congress.

And as the midterms approach, this president’s report card doesn’t look very good. Most Americans give him low marks on just about everything. His approval numbers are under water on foreign policy, on healthcare, on immigration and on the economy, the single most important issue in this and most elections. And then there’s the war the president said would be over in a few weeks.

So 2026 isn’t exactly shaping up to be a banner year for the Republican Party.

But Democrats have problems of their own.

They like to say that theirs is a “big tent” party, one that welcomes candidates with all sorts of opinions and views. Fair enough. Except this year the tent has quite a few people in it whose views Americans probably won’t like — assuming Republicans are smart enough to tell voters what those views actually are.

It’s not exactly breaking news that the energy in the Democratic Party is on the left. Candidates espousing one version or another of socialism have won primary elections, and not only in deep-blue places like New York City.

Republicans will undoubtedly try to make the election about what the Democratic Party’s hard left believes — that America isn’t particularly exceptional, that much of its history is ugly and perhaps irredeemable, and that the country needs to be fundamentally changed.

Key word: fundamentally.

Let’s just say it’s not exactly an upbeat message.

So the midterms may come down not to which candidates voters like more, but which side they detest less: the party that welcomes, however grudgingly, democratic socialists into their big tent along with their message that can sound like America needs a complete overhaul — or the party of Donald Trump, with all the chaos that implies.

Which brings me to another question: Are Republicans better off if Trump leaves the White House, hits the road, and campaigns for Republican candidates — or if he stays put in Washington, and to the extent he’s capable, doesn’t make waves?

The argument for sending him out on the road is obvious. He can rev up the Republican base and encourage Republican voters to turn out. Without him on the campaign trail, the thinking goes, some of those voters might just stay home. So he is constantly telling Republicans: “Pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot.”

But there’s a problem. Trump doesn’t just rev up Republicans. Nobody energizes Democrats more than he does. The more Democrats see him on their local newscasts, the more likely they are to get angry — and angry voters have a funny habit of showing up on Election Day.

It’s true that Democrats don’t need much encouragement this year to get off the couch and vote, such is their fear and loathing of the president. But what about that crucial bloc of voters — independents? They often decide close elections — and they’re hardly charter members of the Trump fan club.

There’s another problem. When Trump headlines a political rally, you sometimes get the impression he has forgotten why he was there. He rambles from one subject to another, inevitably goes off script, and too often says something outrageous that becomes the news of the day.

And suddenly nobody is talking about the Republican candidate he supposedly came to help.

That’s the Trump paradox for Republicans: The man who may be best at getting their voters to the polls may also be the man best at getting everybody else there, too.

My vote? With only a few exceptions, I think the president should stay in Washington and — for a change — concentrate on what voters actually care about, like grocery and gas prices, instead of golden ballrooms and majestic arches.

If he shows up to support a Republican in a tight race, there’s a good chance swing voters will do what swing voters do: Swing the other way.

Sometimes the best campaign contribution a president can make is knowing when not to campaign.

Bernard Goldberg is an Emmy and an Alfred I. duPont-Columbia University award-winning writer and journalist. He is the author of five books and publishes exclusive weekly columns, audio commentaries and Q&As on his Substack page.
